subtopic: Law of Mass Action and Equilibrium Constant
stem:
Write the rate equation for the following reaction:

i. \(\mathrm{C} + \mathrm{O_2} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CO_2}\)

ii. \(2\mathrm{KClO_3} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{KCl} + 3\mathrm{O_2}\)
solution:
The rate equation is written by applying the law of mass action.

i. The reactants are \(\mathrm{C}\) and \(\mathrm{O_2}\)

Rate \(\alpha\ [\mathrm{C}][\mathrm{O_2}]\)

\(\therefore\) Rate \(= k\,[\mathrm{C}][\mathrm{O_2}]\)

ii. The reactant is \(\mathrm{KClO_3}\) and its 2 molecules appear in the balanced equation.

\(\therefore\) Rate \(\alpha\ [\mathrm{KClO_3}]^2\)

\(\therefore\) Rate \(= k\,[\mathrm{KClO_3}]^2\)
_note: p-05 left column, printed p.179. Label printed 'Problem 12.1 :' with a 'Solution :' label.

subtopic: Law of Mass Action and Equilibrium Constant
stem:
\(\mathrm{N_2(g)} + 3\mathrm{H_2(g)} \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{NH_3(g)}\)

Write expression for \(K_P\) in terms of \(K_c\).
solution:
\(K_P = \dfrac{(P_{\mathrm{NH_3}})^2}{(P_{\mathrm{N_2}})(P_{\mathrm{H_2}})^3}\)

\(\therefore K_P = \dfrac{[\mathrm{NH_3(g)}]^2 [RT]^2}{[\mathrm{N_2(g)}]RT \cdot [\mathrm{H_2(g)}]^3 [RT]^3}\)

\(\therefore K_P = \dfrac{[\mathrm{NH_3(g)}]^2}{[\mathrm{N_2(g)}][\mathrm{H_2(g)}]^3} \times \dfrac{[RT]^2}{[RT][RT]^3}\)

\(\therefore K_P = K_C \times RT^{(2-4)}\)

\(\therefore K_P = K_C \times RT^{-2}\)
_note: p-06 right column, printed p.180. Label printed 'Problem  12.2 :' with a DOUBLE space between the word and the number — one of the label variants the brief warns about.

subtopic: Law of Mass Action and Equilibrium Constant
stem:
Write an expression for \(K_P\) and relate it to \(K_c\) for the following reversible reaction.

\(\mathrm{H_2(g)} + \mathrm{I_2(g)} \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{HI(g)}\)
solution:
\(K_P = \dfrac{(P_{\mathrm{HI}})^2}{(P_{\mathrm{H_2}})(P_{\mathrm{I_2}})}\)

\(\therefore K_P = \dfrac{[\mathrm{HI(g)}]^2 [RT]^2}{[\mathrm{H_2(g)}]RT \cdot [\mathrm{I_2(g)}]RT}\)

\(\therefore K_P = \dfrac{[\mathrm{HI(g)}]^2}{[\mathrm{H_2(g)}][\mathrm{I_2(g)}]} \times \dfrac{[RT]^2}{[RT][RT]}\)

\(\therefore K_P = K_C \times RT^{2-(1+1)}\)

\(\therefore K_P = K_C\)

stem: Equal concentrations of hydrogen and iodine are mixed together in a closed container at 700 K and allowed to come to equilibrium. If the concentraion of HI at equilibrium is \(0.85\ \mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}}\), what are the equilibrium concentrations of \(\mathrm{H_2}\) and \(\mathrm{I_2}\) if \(K_C = 54\) at this temperature ?
solution:
Balanced chemical reaction :

\(\mathrm{H_2(g)} + \mathrm{I_2(g)} \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{HI(g)}\)

\(\therefore K_c = \dfrac{[\mathrm{HI(g)}]^2}{[\mathrm{H_2(g)}][\mathrm{I_2(g)}]}\)

on substituting the values

\(\therefore 54 = \dfrac{(0.85)^2}{[\mathrm{H_2(g)}]^2}\)

as initial concentrations of \(\mathrm{H_2(g)}\) and \(\mathrm{I_2(g)}\) are equal.

(Refer to the balanced chemical equation : 1 mole of \(\mathrm{H_2}\) reacts with 1 mole of \(\mathrm{I_2}\))

Equilibrium concentration of \(\mathrm{I_2(g)}\) = Equilibrium concentration of \(\mathrm{H_2(g)}\)

\(\therefore 54 = \dfrac{(0.85)^2}{[\mathrm{H_2(g)}]^2}\)

\(\therefore [\mathrm{H_2(g)}] = 0.12\ \mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}}\)

Equilibrium concentrations of \(\mathrm{H_2}\) and \(\mathrm{I_2}\) are equal to \(0.12\ \mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}}\).
_note: Stem on p-10 left column, solution completes in the p-10 RIGHT column (printed p.184) — the one worked example here that straddles a column break. The book prints 'concentraion' in the stem; transcribed as printed. Arithmetic checked: 0.7225/54 = 0.013380, square root 0.1157, which rounds to the printed 0.12.

stem:
The equilibrium constant \(K_C\) for the reaction of hydrogen with iodine is 54.0 at 700 K.

\(\mathrm{H_2(g)} + \mathrm{I_2(g)} \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{HI(g)}\)

\(K_C = 54.0\) at 700 K

a. If \(k_f\) is the rate constant for the formation of HI and \(k_r\) is the rate constant for the decomposition of HI, deduce whether \(k_f\) is larger or smaller than \(k_r\).

b. If the value of \(k_r\) at 700 K is \(1.16 \times 10^{-3}\), what is the \(k_f\) ?
solution:
a. As \(K_C = \dfrac{k_f}{k_r} = 54.0\),

\(k_f\) is greater than \(k_r\) by a factor of 54.0

b. \(K_f = K_C \times k_r = 54.0 \times (1.16 \times 10^{-3})\)

\(= 62.64 \times 10^{-3}\)
_note: p-11 left column, printed p.185. In the printed reaction k_f is set above the forward arrow and k_r below the reverse arrow; those labels are NOT reproduced in the stem because part (a) of the book's own question already defines both constants, so nothing is lost and nothing is added. Publisher-report item (not bracketed, changes no answer): part b prints a CAPITAL 'K_f' where the lowercase rate constant k_f belongs, and gives no unit; 62.64 x 10^-3 is arithmetically correct (54.0 x 1.16e-3 = 0.06264).

_note: Printed 'equlilibrium' (the book's own misspelling) and the hydroxide ion is printed WITHOUT its negative charge, as OH(aq). Both transcribed as printed; neither changes the answer.
solution: [Textbook misprint: two printing defects in this stem, neither of which changes the answer. (i) The hydroxide ion is printed as \(\mathrm{OH(aq)}\), with NO negative charge; it should be \(\mathrm{OH^{\ominus}(aq)}\), since the equation must balance in charge as well as in atoms and the book itself writes \(\mathrm{H^{\oplus}}\) with its charge on the same line. Preserved as printed. (ii) The state symbol on water is typeset as an ITALIC DIGIT ONE, so the page reads \(\mathrm{H_2O(1)}\); confirmed from the PDF's own font data, where the character is the digit 1 in Times New Roman Italic. It is plainly the italic letter \(l\) for liquid, and is transcribed here as \(\mathrm{H_2O(l)}\) because "(1)" is not a state symbol at all and would read as nonsense.]

stem: The relation between \(K_c\) and \(K_p\) for the reaction \(\mathrm{A(g)} + \mathrm{B(g)} \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{C(g)} + \mathrm{D(g)}\) is
_note: Option (a) is printed literally as 'Kc = Ykp' — a capital letter Y with NO overbar, verified at 9x against option (c) on the same line, which carries a proper radical sign with an overbar. Almost certainly a misprint for the square root, which would make (a) and (b) the SAME statement. As printed no option is strictly correct: the reaction has dn = 3 - 2 = +1, so Kp = Kc(RT) and Kp/Kc = RT. (D) is keyed because it is the only option stating a genuine Kp-Kc relation of the form the chapter derives (Kp = Kc(RT)^dn with dn = 0), and it is what a mis-count of dn as 0 produces. Full explanation goes in the errata bracket.
solution: [Textbook misprint: as printed, NO option is strictly correct. The reaction \(\mathrm{A(g)} + \mathrm{B(g)} \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{C(g)} + \mathrm{D(g)}\) has 2 moles of gas on the left and 3 on the right, so \(\Delta n = +1\) and this chapter's own Eq. 12.7 gives \(K_P = K_C(RT)\), i.e. \(K_p/K_c = RT\), not 1. Option (d) is the answer intended and is what the general relation gives whenever \(\Delta n = 0\), which is very likely how the question was written — counting two species on each side rather than the moles. Separately, option (a) is printed as "\(K_c = \mathrm{Y}k_p\)", with a capital letter Y carrying no overbar, against option (c) on the same line which carries a proper radical sign; it is evidently a misprint for \(K_c = \sqrt{K_p}\), which would make options (a) and (b) the same statement rearranged and so rule out both. Both defects preserved as printed.]

stem: When volume of the equilibrium reaction \(\mathrm{C(g)} + \mathrm{H_2O(g)} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{CO(g)} + \mathrm{H_2(g)}\) is increased at constant temperature the equilibrium will
_note: The book prints carbon as C(g). Solved AS PRINTED: 2 mol of gas on each side, dn = 0, so a volume change cannot shift it. If carbon were the solid it actually is in this (water-gas) reaction the gaseous moles would run 1 to 2 and the answer would be (a) — flagged in the errata bracket rather than silently re-solved.
solution: [Textbook misprint: carbon is printed as a GAS, \(\mathrm{C(g)}\). This is the water-gas reaction, in which carbon is a solid, and the state symbol here is answer-affecting. As printed there are 2 moles of gas on each side, \(\Delta n = 0\), and a change of volume cannot move the equilibrium — which is the answer keyed above, since the rule of this bank is to solve the question exactly as the book prints it. With \(\mathrm{C(s)}\), the solid would be left out of the equilibrium expression, the gaseous moles would run 1 to 2, and increasing the volume would shift the equilibrium from left to right, making the option that reads "shift from left to right" the correct one instead. Preserved as printed, with both readings stated in the solution.]
